from day one JPMorgan sees bitcoin capitulation in record Strategy discount, but 3 risks cloud the call Five questions over Nvidia's China chip trail that Huang's return has not settled NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears Tokyo CPI preview: core inflation seen jumping to 3% three weeks before BoJ decision US Thanksgiving holiday: European stocks surge, S&P 500 futures finish higher in Thanksgiving trading EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report CoreWeave bond yields are approaching 19%. Why even stock investors should pay attention EUR/USD might be bottoming out amid peak Fed hawkishness and dovish repricing risks Summary: US equity futures rallied, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 2.4%, and Korean chip stocks led Asia higher, with the Kosdaq up around 6.7% Tokyo core CPI rose to a 16-month high of 2.9%, keeping a December BoJ hike in play, though the BoJ's trend gauge eased to 2.5% The US dollar softened, with the Australian and New Zealand dollars edging higher The IMF urged the RBA to stand ready to hike further, while OCBC sees the Aussie's upside capped New Zealand's official count confirmed a hung parliament China's cabinet pledged new capital market support and a bigger role for the national team, while industrial profits rose 20.1% Gold rose about 1.9% to around $3,630 and silver jumped nearly 5%, as strategists split on whether the metal has bottomed Markets overview Risk appetite improved through the Asian session on Friday after a bruising week for AI-linked assets. US equity index futures led the way, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 2.4% and S&P 500 futures about 1.7% higher. South Korea's chip-heavy markets were the standout in Asia: the Kosdaq jumped around 6.7% and the Kospi gained close to 4%, as SK Hynix rose about 4.6% and Samsung Electronics about 4.2%. Japan's Nikkei 225 added around 1.9% to near 58,600, and the Topix rose about 1.8%. Gains in China were more modest, with the Hang Seng up around 0.9% and the Shanghai Composite edging up about 0.3%. US 10-year Treasury yields rose about 7 basis points to around 4.91%. Japan Tokyo's core inflation rate climbed to 2.9% in November, its fastest pace in 16 months, from 2.6% in October, although it came in just below the 3.0% forecast. The Bank of Japan's preferred trend measure, which excludes fresh food and energy, eased to 2.5% from 2.6%, suggesting energy accounted for much of the rise. The data keep a December rate hike as the base case, with markets expecting the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 1.5% at its December 17-18 meeting. Nationwide CPI arrives only hours before that decision. USD/JPY was little changed near 159.20, while the two-year JGB yield held near 1.76%. Australia and New Zealand The US dollar softened against the antipodean currencies, with AUD/USD up about 0.35% to around 0.6660 and NZD/USD up about 0.3% to around 0.5485. The IMF urged the Reserve Bank of Australia to stand ready to raise rates further if inflation proves persistent, citing risks from Middle East energy prices and the danger of inflation expectations becoming unanchored. It also pressed the government to deliver on spending restraint. OCBC took a different view, arguing that the RBA is close to the end of its tightening cycle as the labour market softens, and that the Australian dollar's upside will be increasingly capped as Australia's rate advantage narrows. In New Zealand, official election results confirmed a hung parliament, with the centre-right coalition needing the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The currency market took the result in its stride. Earlier, New Zealand consumer confidence rose to 100.2, its highest since January, as falling fuel prices eased inflation expectations. China China's cabinet pledged new incremental policies for its capital markets, a stronger role for the state-backed national team in stabilising stocks, tighter defences against imported risks, and more dividends and buybacks from listed companies. It gave no details on the size or timing of the support. Industrial profits rose 20.1% from a year earlier in October, up from 14.4% in September, but the gains were concentrated in electronics, with weak household demand and the property downturn still weighing on consumer-facing industries. Gold and commodities Gold rebounded about 1.9% to around $3,630 an ounce, rising even as US yields climbed, while silver jumped nearly 5% to around $43. Views on the metal remain divided. HSBC warned that further equity weakness could push gold through major support at $3,400, while Saxo's Ole Hansen pointed to signs of selling exhaustion. Commonwealth Bank of Australia said the dollar, already near its expected peak, will drive gold in the coming months, and it sees limited downside, with a year-end range of $3,500 to $3,700. Separately, the Reserve Bank of India bought no gold in the six months to September but moved about 60 tonnes home from overseas vaults. Oil edged higher, with Brent up about 0.7% to around $92 a barrel and WTI up about 1% to near $86. OCBC expects the rupee to strengthen as oil eases, forecasting USD/INR at 92.10 by the end of 2027. Also on our radar SpaceX will issue new Class A stock to every US child with an active Trump Account, and Elon Musk pledged to personally match the gift once his lockup ends in June, doubling last month's pledge as total program deposits passed $9 billion. CNBC later reported that SpaceX shares rose on an alternative trading platform. Bitcoin rose almost 1% to around $61,500, after JPMorgan flagged a record discount at Strategy as a possible capitulation signal. Goldman Sachs research argued that the largest US hyperscalers can still earn returns of 15% or more on their AI spending, though specialist neoclouds face more risk. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa and Eurowings resume Dubai flights in November
articles.desc: Dubai: Dubai International Airport has strengthened its international flight network during November, with four European airlines resuming their operations to Dubai - British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa and Eurowings - by restarting flights connecting the emirate with a number of major European c
articles.content: Dubai: Dubai International Airport has strengthened its international flight network during November, with four European airlines resuming their operations to Dubai - British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa and Eurowings - by restarting flights connecting the emirate with a number of major European cities, coinciding with the winter travel season. British Airways resumed flights between London Heathrow and Dubai International Airport from November 3, with one flight per day, while Air France restarted its flights between Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport and Dubai from November 19. On November 25, Lufthansa resumed its flights between Munich and Dubai with five flights per week, while Eurowings restarted its daily flights between Berlin and Dubai, thus adding more direct travel options between Dubai and Germany. The return of the four companies comes as part of restoring air connectivity with European markets and expanding flight options for travellers to and from Dubai, with the arrival of the winter season, which usually sees an increase in travel and tourism. In recent times, other airlines have resumed their flights, including Philippine Airlines, Air Astana, and the Greek airline Aegean, which has resumed its flights between Athens and Dubai. The previous period also witnessed the return of Russian, Turkish and Cypriot airlines, along with a number of other airlines that have resumed their flights, including Royal Air Maroc, SunExpress and Cebu Pacific, while other airlines are scheduled to resume their operations in the coming weeks. Dubai International Airport is currently connected to 235 destinations in 101 countries via 57 airlines, and Dubai International Airport welcomed 50.4 million passengers during the first nine months of 2026.

articles.content: As Candace Owens and Alex Jones make cash spouting conspiracies, let’s give thanks to true US heroes — scientists - Measles | Opinion News As Candace Owens and Alex Jones make cash spouting conspiracies, let’s give thanks to true US heroes — scientists American life expectancy rose from 47 to 79 thanks to science. As anti-science views spread, remember the pioneers who made modern life safe. Do you think the conspiracy theorists, anti-vaxxers and science denying ghouls ever consider the irony of their lives? On reflection, probably not. They wake up in air-conditioned bedrooms made possible by science, drink water that won’t give them cholera, pour pasteurized milk into their coffee, take medication for their blood pressure, check the weather forecast via GPS, and then sit in front of a computer — made possible by great minds like Babbage and Turing — to explain why scientists don’t know what they’re talking about. You see this shtick everywhere, and not just from Russian and Chinese bots seeking to weaken America’s faith in one of its greatest contributions to the world. Gwyneth Paltrow marketed healing energy stickers not on the basis of evidence but intuition. She also promoted vaginal jade eggs, goat’s milk parasite cleanse and rectal ozone therapy . Shailene Woodley said we should eat clay to remove heavy metals — a conclusion she drew after a conversation with a taxi driver. Mel Gibson has argued for anti-parasitic drugs as cancer treatments . The track covers hundreds of everyday tasks given as plain-language instructions, including closing drawers, moving baskets and scrunching towels. The task-completion percentages describe this benchmark comparison, not reliability across everything a robot might encounter. articles.title: Indie web browser Ladybird enters alpha testing
articles.desc: Upstart engine gets downloadable macOS and Linux builds, but no security guarantees
articles.content: Indie web browser Ladybird enters alpha testing Indie web browser Ladybird enters alpha testing Upstart engine gets downloadable macOS and Linux builds, but no security guarantees Debian wakes up wearing Windows XP's actual skin Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz The independent Ladybird web browser has reached an important milestone: an alpha test version. What's more, it works well. These may not be the criteria by which some will judge it, though. Earlier this week, the developer behind the Ladybird web browser announced that . We've given it a brief test, and it performed very well. It's more stable and works better than its alpha label would suggest. , covering macOS on Apple Silicon, as well as for Linux on x86-64; for the latter, there's a Flatpak package, as well as native Ubuntu and Fedora packages. It's an open source project, so you can download the source code from the and compile it yourself, but in an unusual move, back in June the project announced that the developers would no longer accept public code contributions. We first mentioned Ladybird as part of our early 2022 look at its original parent project – SerenityOS: Remarkable project with its own JS-capable web browser . Both the name and the date are significant: the former is a nod to the , recited at the end of Alcoholics Anonymous meetings. The date of the article is because it's well before the About a year and a half later, we reported that Serenity OS turns five and emits first offspring, Ladybird . Both the OS and the browser were still hand-coded, but now the browser could be compiled and run on other OSes. That freed it up to call upon external libraries which didn't exist for SerenityOS. Ladybird flutters toward Rust with a little help from AI used Apple's Swift language, but this year, he changed course and adopted Rust instead, using LLM tools to convert some existing code. Some will dismiss Ladybird because of this, but as our first coverage shows, the browser and its original host OS were established projects before the current wave of AI-assisted development. Kling does use LLMs, but Ladybird is not some sloppy vibe-coded effort. The macOS download is 68.4 MB in size, which in 2026 is remarkably small. The Flatpak is larger – about 111 MB – but it also pulls in some KDE dependencies which increase its size. We tested it on Pop!_OS. It handles sites such as and Hacker News and everything else we tried perfectly, and took just 6 percent of our Dell XPS13's CPU to play full-screen HD video from YouTube smoothly. In our short testing, we saw no crashes, hesitation, or any other problems at all. The developers nevertheless warn that the alpha can crash, some websites will not work, and they make no security guarantees at this stage. The use of LLMs will put some people off. However, this is not the only controversial thing about the project. As we have noted in our previous coverage, Ladybird belongs to the same political wing of the FOSS movement as Omarchy, XLibre, and other right-wing projects. If the LLM use doesn't put you off, the political views may. On the other hand, as we've seen from our earlier coverage of Omarchy and XLibre, the same factors also attract others. The modern Web is an entire complex compute platform in its own right, and currently, only three tools support it – and two of those are interrelated. The dominant engines are Google's Blink, used by Chrome and other Chromium browsers; Apple's WebKit, used by Safari; and Mozilla's Gecko, used by Firefox. Blink was forked from WebKit. matures some more, it may be another. Even so, today, the first preliminary release of Ladybird means that there are now four competitive modern browser engines. articles.title: The South Pole Telescope Has Produced Its Sharpest-Ever View of the Universe's Hidden Matter
articles.desc: A new map built from South Pole Telescope observations offers the clearest view yet of how matter is distributed across the universe.
articles.content: The South Pole Telescope Has Produced Its Sharpest-Ever View of the Universe's Hidden Matter Astronomers have reconstructed the most sensitive map of cosmic matter yet using ancient light from the early universe, offering a new way to investigate how galaxies, large-scale structures and the universe itself evolved over billions of years. Built from observations collected by the in Antarctica, the map measures how gravity bends the (CMB), bringing scientists closer to answering some of cosmology’s most persistent questions. An Unprecedented Map Built From Ancient Light The new results come from observations made during the 2019 and 2020 observing seasons with the third-generation camera of the South Pole Telescope, known as , the dataset provides an exceptionally detailed measurement of gravitational lensing across a substantial region of the observable universe. The research, led by scientists from approximately 30 institutions, uses the faint afterglow of as a background against which the distribution of matter can be reconstructed. This radiation has traveled through space for more than 13 billion years, crossing regions containing galaxies, galaxy clusters and other concentrations of matter before reaching Earth. Along the way, gravity slightly changes its trajectory, leaving measurable distortions in the original signal. By identifying those distortions, researchers can infer how matter is distributed between the early universe and the present day. The resulting reconstruction offers a different perspective from traditional astronomical surveys, which generally rely on observing visible galaxies and galaxy clusters. “This is the deepest map of the universe we have so far—it’s like taking a photograph with very low background noise exposure,” said Yuuki Omori, a research scientist at the University of Chicago and lead author of the paper, which was posted to the How Gravitational Lensing Reveals Invisible Matter The technique behind the discovery relies on of general relativity. Massive objects curve spacetime, causing light traveling near them to follow slightly distorted paths. Although the effect is often discussed in connection with distant galaxies appearing stretched or magnified, it also affects the cosmic microwave background. The CMB originated when the universe became transparent to light, approximately 380,000 years after the Big B ang. Since then, its radiation has crossed almost the entire observable universe. Every massive structure along its journey has contributed to the gravitational distortions that scientists can now measure. The SPT-3G researchers reconstructed these distortions using measurements of both the temperature and polarization of microwave radiation. Their analysis combines different components of the signal through a mathematical technique called a , allowing them to extract the gravitational lensing information with exceptional sensitivity. Amy Bender, an Argonne physicist and co-author of the study, explained why this measurement offers a distinct scientific advantage. “This measurement gives us a powerful way to study how matter has gathered into structure over cosmic time. Because it is based on the gravitational lensing of the CMB, it provides an important view of the universe that complements measurements of galaxies and galaxy clusters,” she said. The research also benefited from computing resources at the and Argonne’s Crossover cluster. These systems helped scientists process the telescope observations and test their reconstruction methods against simulated microwave images. “The quality of these data allowed us to reconstruct the lensing signal with extraordinary precision,” said Wei Quan, a postdoctoral appointee at Argonne and a co-author of the paper. “This analysis depends on carefully processing the raw data obtained from the telescope and testing the result against realistic simulations. He made the remarks during a meeting with young artificial intelligence talents held as part of the international conference “AI Journey 2026: A Journey into the World of Artificial Intelligence,” organized by Sberbank in Moscow. “Nowadays, everyone uses smartphones, but for some reason, many people think they are only meant for making calls, sending messages, or watching movies. And then there is TikTok. TikTok is a dangerous thing that destroys the human brain, especially that of young people,” Tokayev said. According to the president, Kazakhstan aims to develop a people-oriented digital economy. He stressed that the effective use of smartphones and access to the internet provide opportunities to earn money even for people living in rural areas and small towns. “However, if you use a smartphone properly and skillfully, you can earn money even while living in a village or a small settlement. All you need is internet access,” he noted. Tokayev also highlighted the importance of providing relevant training to citizens, enabling them to generate legitimate income through digital technologies. “This is what I call a ‘people’s digital economy,’” the Kazakh president added. © 2026 Trend News Agency.
